title: France wrote ‘Paris time minus 9 minutes 21 seconds’ into law instead of saying Greenwich
hook: France's 1911 time law never says Greenwich

open.title: Why France deliberately set its clocks back 9 minutes 21 seconds
open.line: March 1911: France passed a one-line time law.

summary: In 1911 France set legal time as Paris mean time minus 9 minutes 21 seconds: Greenwich time without the name.

text: In March 1911, French law set the time as:
Paris mean time, delayed by 9 minutes 21 seconds.
That's roughly the Paris to Greenwich time gap.
Yet the text never says Greenwich.

panels.text: Why not just write Greenwich time?

text: In 1884, a conference voted Greenwich 0 degrees longitude.
France abstained. Only Santo Domingo voted no.
Actually, an 1896 bill had named Greenwich outright.
A year later, a deputy recast it as 9 minutes 21 seconds.
With Greenwich hidden, the lower house passed it without debate.
Stuck in the Senate, it passed only in March 1911.
At 12 midnight on the 10th, Paris public clocks paused 9 minutes 21 seconds.
But 9 minutes 21 seconds was 0.065 seconds off the real observatory gap.
It stayed in law until UTC replaced it in 1978.
